storyboard.claim: By invoking Dante and Petrarch, Humbert reframes his obsession as literary destiny, not crime.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert addresses the jury with the shield icon — literary allusions used as armor against conviction.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues from the Dante/Petrarch strategy (context beats 37-39): now the payoff of that alignment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shield makes the defensive purpose visible; the strike-through rejects the claim for the viewer.

storyboard.claim: Humbert positions himself as a victim of the same poetic fate as Dante — a grand romantic destiny.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert alone against an abstract backdrop, performing the grand claim the struck-through text rejects.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Elaborates beat 40's shield defense: the specific phrase he hides behind.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through tells the muted viewer this phrase is a lie the hosts are dismantling.

storyboard.claim: A host pauses: if Humbert knows he is doomed and will die in prison, what is the actual point of the confession?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sits in the prison cell — the confined man whose motive for writing is the question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Interrupts the analysis of Humbert's strategy to ask why he bothers at all.
storyboard.addedInformation: Placing him in the cell grounds the question: he is already caught, so what does the confession serve?

storyboard.claim: Is the confession sincere or is it the ultimate arrogant brag from a con artist proving he is the smartest in the courtroom?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert smirks in the courtroom — the arrogant face of a man enjoying his own performance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers beat 42's question with a hypothesis: this is vanity, not remorse.
storyboard.addedInformation: The smirk tells the muted viewer this man is pleased with himself, not contrite.

storyboard.claim: The confession is entirely a brag disguised as a confession — he performs remorse but the performance is purely aesthetic.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert wears a sad face beside the mask icon — the grief is worn, not felt.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms beat 43's hypothesis: this IS a con artist's brag.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask + performed sadness together tell the muted viewer the emotion is fake — a costume, not a feeling.

storyboard.claim: Humbert does not want forgiveness — he wants to be admired for the beauty of how he confesses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert's vain, pleased expression as he addresses the court — admiration is the real goal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the fake remorse (44) to his true motive: applause, not absolution.
storyboard.addedInformation: The happy face after the sad mask of beat 44 shows the real emotion underneath the performance.

storyboard.claim: He dares the jury to convict a man who can write so beautifully — the prose IS the defense.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holds the manuscript, his weapon: the beautiful writing that dares the jury to convict.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The logical conclusion of beats 43-45: what his performance actually demands from the jury.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes in hand make the manuscript visible as the instrument of his defense.

storyboard.claim: Every literary allusion and poetic rhythm is a smoke bomb to disorient the reader — and Nabokov is actively testing you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — the literary allusions are a disguise. Nabokov stands beside a worried Humbert, pointing: the deception is exposed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from Humbert's motive (45-46) to Nabokov's design: the game is the author's, not just the character's.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask icon + worried expression tells the muted viewer someone is hiding behind a false face, not celebrating.

storyboard.claim: The more educated you are, the more susceptible you become — recognizing the references creates kinship with the narrator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov points at the funnel-trap icon: education funnels the reader into the trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the mechanism of beat 47's game: how exactly the smoke bomb works.
storyboard.addedInformation: The funnel-trap makes the mechanism visible — the reader's knowledge is what pulls them in.

storyboard.claim: If you get the Dante reference, you feel smart — and then you are already on Humbert's side.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert's satisfied face in the courtroom: he has won the educated reader over without them noticing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The result of beat 48's funnel: the reader lands on the predator's side.
storyboard.addedInformation: His pleased expression shows the trap has closed — the reader's complicity is secured.

storyboard.claim: The central question: will you allow aesthetic beauty to override your basic moral judgment?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram showing aesthetic beauty leading to moral override — the mechanism of the novel distilled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Crystallizes the trap described in beats 47-49 into a single structural diagram.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram makes the cause-and-effect explicit: beauty is not a neutral quality, it is a weapon aimed at your judgment.

storyboard.claim: Humbert needs a sympathetic origin story, and he constructs one around his childhood sweetheart Annabel Lee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert reaches toward Annabel on the shore — the manufactured romantic origin made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Beat 50 asked why he needs beauty as a weapon; this answers with his first move: a tragic backstory.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing both characters together introduces Annabel and stages the 'lost love' narrative Humbert constructs.

storyboard.claim: They met in 1919 on the Riviera — an elaborately staged romantic setting.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Annabel walk along the shore, happy — the nostalgic scene Humbert paints for the jury.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues beat 51: the origin story unfolds in its picturesque setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the visual stages Humbert's version faithfully; the word 'setup' in the callout hints it is constructed.

storyboard.claim: Before they consummate the relationship, Annabel dies of typhus — and Humbert blames his entire adult life on this tragedy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Annabel collapses on the shore beside the grave icon; Humbert slumps in performed grief.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The Riviera romance (52) ends in death — the pivot of Humbert's origin story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grave icon + the death callout make the tragedy literal for a muted viewer.

storyboard.claim: Humbert claims 'Lolita began with Annabel' and borrows Edgar Allan Poe's poem Annabel Lee to frame the connection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holds a book in the library — literally borrowing from literature to make his case.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After Annabel's death (53), Humbert draws the line to Dolores — the hosts reject this with a strike.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book icon makes the literary borrowing concrete; the strike-through tells viewers the claim is false.

storyboard.claim: Humbert borrows Poe's grief to dress up his own predation — he wants the jury to pity him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holds the book with a sad face beside the mask icon — the grief is borrowed, the sadness performed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens beat 54: not just citing Poe but wearing his grief as a disguise.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask + performed sadness together show the muted viewer that this grief is a costume, not genuine feeling.

storyboard.claim: Humbert frames his condition as eternal arrested development — a man frozen in time by teenage heartbreak.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert stands motionless in an abstract void, performing the paralysis he claims defines him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The emotional conclusion of the Annabel strategy (51-55): what the origin story is supposed to prove.
storyboard.addedInformation: His idle stance and sad expression stage the claim physically — a man who appears stuck.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's narrative: 'I am not a predator making active choices — I am just a man with a broken heart trying to recapture lost love.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert addresses the court with a sad face, performing innocence — the strike-through rejects the claim.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the full version of the defense beats 51-56 have built up.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through does the critical work: without sound, the viewer reads the words being explicitly rejected.

storyboard.claim: It is like a comic-book villain writing their own tragic origin story — a defense attorney tampering with emotional evidence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in the prison cell holding his manuscript, performing vulnerability as he writes his own myth.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes beats 51-57 in a single dismissive comparison: this is a villain's self-authored myth.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through tells the muted viewer: even 'tragic origin story' is rejected — it is pure fabrication.

storyboard.claim: Humbert builds a beautiful facade over a structurally condemned building and begs the reader not to examine the foundation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert points away from something — directing attention elsewhere, the con artist's misdirection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the fabricated origin (51-58) to the structural metaphor: what holds it up is rotten.
storyboard.addedInformation: His pointing gesture makes the misdirection physical — he is literally directing the viewer's gaze away.

storyboard.claim: The foundation of the Annabel defense is rotten — the beautiful arch is built on something that cannot hold.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in the abstract void, no icon — the callout alone carries the revelation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes beat 59's metaphor: what he told you not to look at is exactly what is wrong.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging is minimal — the callout does the work, echoing the previous beat's warning.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov leaves the receipts lying around — evidence that the origin story is fabricated, hidden in plain sight for the careful reader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov points at the magnifier icon: close examination reveals what Humbert tries to hide.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts credit from the rotten foundation (60) to the architect who planted the evidence: Nabokov.
storyboard.addedInformation: Magnifier makes 'close reading' visual; Nabokov's presence names the author as the one leaving clues.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov allows Humbert to spin the romantic yarn but forces the careful reader to notice where Humbert slips up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov stands behind Humbert, pointing at him — the architect catching his own character in a lie.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Nabokov's planted evidence (61) to the specific moment: Humbert's mask fails.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two-character staging shows author and character in the same frame — the puppeteer and his creation.

storyboard.claim: Humbert claims he was paralyzed by grief, incapable of adult romance — the hosts reject this.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert slumps in the courtroom performing paralysis — the strike-through brands the claim a lie.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates the specific claim (from 56-57) that Nabokov's evidence (61-62) will now dismantle.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through paired with performed grief tells the muted viewer: this sadness is an act being exposed.

storyboard.claim: During Humbert's European period, the mask slips completely — long before America or Dolores, his true nature shows.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert on a European street with a caught expression — the mask slipping off.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Beat 63 stated the false claim; this beat shows the moment Nabokov lets it crack.
storyboard.addedInformation: The surprised expression stages the 'slip' — Humbert's composure breaks and the truth shows through.

storyboard.claim: During his supposed grief period, Humbert was actively stalking children in Paris parks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walks a European street with a cold, calculating expression — not frozen in grief but on the prowl.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The first piece of Nabokov's evidence (from 61-62): what 'paralyzed by grief' actually looked like.
storyboard.addedInformation: His neutral, focused face contrasts beat 63's performed sadness — the same man, unmasked.

storyboard.claim: He describes sitting on a park bench pretending to read a book while watching children.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sits holding a book — not reading it, using it as a prop to disguise what he is doing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms into the park scene from beat 65: the specific image Nabokov gives us.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book in hand makes 'pretending' concrete — the intellectual prop is physically visible.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's own words: 'my book for fig leaf' — literature literally and metaphorically covering his predation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sits with the book held in front of him — the book icon reinforces the physical object as a shield.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The damning punchline of beat 66's park-bench scene: the book is not intellectual, it is a cover.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book icon makes the object central; the callout names its function — a fig leaf, not literature.

storyboard.claim: That phrase dismantles his entire defense — he uses literature to literally and metaphorically cover his predation in public parks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing, holding the book as an instrument — literature reduced to a covering device.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands beat 67's quote into the systemic insight: literature is always his cover story.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: similar staging to 67; the callout shift from 'fig leaf' to 'literature to cover' widens the meaning.

storyboard.claim: There is no romantic destiny here — only calculated predatory behavior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walks the street with a cold, purposeful face — no trace of the grieving romantic.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on the park-bench evidence (65-68): what he is, stripped of the prose.
storyboard.addedInformation: His neutral, deliberate walk visually opposes the slumping grief of beat 63 — the contrast is the proof.

storyboard.claim: Humbert casually mentions interactions with a young Parisian street walker named Monique.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in a Parisian cafe setting — the European backdrop where a second piece of evidence surfaces.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A new receipt after the park bench (65-69): another incident that dismantles the Annabel defense.
storyboard.addedInformation: Naming the scene gives the muted viewer a landmark in the evidence chain.

storyboard.claim: Monique claims she is 18, but Humbert deduces she is younger and takes immense sadistic pleasure in that realization.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert with a satisfied, sinister expression — this is not joy but the pleasure of a predator confirmed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The detail from the Monique scene (70): what Humbert actually feels is predatory satisfaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: His pleased face is deliberately unsettling: the muted viewer sees a man happy about something the callout names as sadistic.

storyboard.claim: Humbert marries his first wife Valeria but admits he only tolerated her because she gave an imitation of a little girl.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in a domestic bedroom, cold and detached — the marriage was never about the woman.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Third receipt after the park bench (65-69) and Monique (70-71): the pattern is now undeniable.
storyboard.addedInformation: The bedroom set makes the domestic context real; his neutral expression shows he feels nothing for the wife.

storyboard.claim: He stole a child's nightgown from an orphanage and forced his adult wife to wear it so he could pretend.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holds an unseen object in the bedroom — the cruelty of the detail staged through his cold composure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens beat 72: not just a psychological preference but a concrete, planned act of cruelty.
storyboard.addedInformation: His casual holding gesture and flat expression make the calculated cruelty visible — no remorse, no hesitation.

storyboard.claim: The Annabel story is nothing more than a convenient fiction — the evidence proves he was a predator long before any lost love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and the ghost of Annabel in abstract space — the strike-through crosses out the entire origin story.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Verdict on all the evidence (65-73): the origin story is definitively debunked.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing Annabel one last time with the strike-through makes the dismissal visual: she was never the reason.

storyboard.claim: He was a fully formed, active predator in Europe — not waiting for a ghost but actively seeking victims.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walks with cold purpose on a European street — a predator in motion, not a grieving man frozen in time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The summary of beats 64-74: this is who he was the entire time.
storyboard.addedInformation: His deliberate stride directly contradicts the frozen-in-time claim from beat 56.

storyboard.claim: He used adult women as 'palliative agents' — a temporary fix — and by the time he reaches America, his pathology is a finely tuned engine.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert on the highway heading toward America — his pathology travels with him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridge from Europe (64-75) to America: his predation is not a crisis but a system.
storyboard.addedInformation: The highway set signals transit — the predator is on the move to new territory.

storyboard.claim: In America, he needs a host family to infiltrate — a place to stay and a target to access.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking toward a suburban street beside the funnel-trap icon: he is setting a trap, not seeking a home.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Arrives in America (76) and immediately seeks a target — the predator's method continues.
storyboard.addedInformation: The funnel-trap icon makes the infiltration strategy visible: the family is being funneled into his plan.

storyboard.claim: Instead of hiding in shadows, he walks into the brightly lit postwar American suburbs — the cynical European predator meets naive America.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert strides confidently into a suburban street — the collision between predator and open, trusting landscape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The surprise of beat 77: he does the opposite of hiding.
storyboard.addedInformation: The street set stages the American suburb; his confident walk shows he feels no need to conceal himself here.

storyboard.claim: The collision gives us Charlotte Haze and 342 Lawn Street in Ramsdale — some of the most masterful and disturbing chapters in the novel.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte greets Humbert in the boarding-house parlor — the home icon marks the specific address.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The predator (75-78) finds his target: a specific house, a specific woman, a specific child inside.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's eager, happy expression introduces her character immediately — trying too hard to impress the European lodger.
